item.content:encoded:
Cosign, a16z's bet, argues that the next chapter in hiring isn't mass-applying for jobs—it's having someone you trust, or eventually your own AI agent, run the first round of screening for you.

The episode leans toward product introduction and award promotion, but the idea of agents negotiating on behalf of both sides first deserves close study from anyone following the AI-plus-hiring space.

2:07 Talent data gets trapped inside corporate silos, invisible across companies
Sophia observes that knowledge of who's a growth expert or top engineer usually stays confined to each company or small circle, never crossing organizational boundaries. Dhruv responds that Cosign Awards aims to break down these silos—transforming what companies normally keep quiet through internal gossip (like ‘which company has the highest talent density’ or ‘which product had the biggest impact this year’) into searchable public information, not just awards for famous founders and CEOs.

5:15 Niche award categories surface far more talented people than expected
David cites specific numbers: the public intellectual category has 65 nominations, podcaster of the year has 76, and Rising Stars—his personal favorite—already has 135 nominations, currently the largest category. None of these align with traditional job titles, revealing a massive population of people with strong internal company reputations but no public visibility, who need a window to be seen.

8:15 The real product isn't the network—it's your surface area for serendipity
David quotes Jobs: you can't plan to meet the person who changes your life, but you can place yourself on the path where luck travels and grab the opportunity when it appears. He applies this to Cosign—building profiles, populating the graph, browsing relationships—is fundamentally increasing the odds that future partners or the right person will spot you. He calls this ‘coincidence of intent’: when two people with complementary skills wanting to build the same thing can actually be matched by the system.

14:27 Three layers build the complete graph: profiles, lists, then co-signs
David breaks Cosign into three layers. The bottom is a Wikipedia-like profile system for 40,000 to 50,000 people, clickable through companies and investors. The middle layer is ‘lists’—about 400 people have published lists so far, like Packy McCormick's 36 companies he thinks are worth joining. The top layer is ‘co-sign’ itself, where someone formally tells the platform ‘I'd work with this person anywhere.’ All three together form the complete graph.

17:39 LinkedIn's search limits are a choice, not a technical constraint
Dhruv believes LinkedIn will never open an MCP that enables full-text search across its entire relationship graph—even with hundreds of thousands of accounts, ordinary users still can't find the people they need. He recounts his own experience: hunting for startups worth joining in New York, he asked Gemini, then ChatGPT, and both gave poor answers. His conclusion: factual ‘who's doing what’ questions fail because the underlying data simply doesn't exist. Cosign's graph, fed by real professional relationships, fills that gap.

19:41 The next frontier: agents that negotiate on your behalf, not just write emails
Dhruv notes the personal-agent wave lasted only a month or two; Muse hit 10 million users, but even the most tailored agent today can only draft an email in your inbox, send it to theirs, and wait for their agent to pick it up and reply—essentially the old ‘send message, wait for response’ loop. He points to early examples like Instagon where agent-to-agent protocols are already emerging (such as car-rental customer-service integrations), imagining the future: when job hunting, your agent could negotiate a round with the company's agent, assess whether your intentions align, and only then decide whether to surface you to the actual hiring manager.

21:42 Everyone's inbox treats all signals equally—and that's the core problem to solve
Dhruv points out that in today's social networks, Sam Altman's inbox and a regular person's inbox—even his 14-year-old sister's—work exactly the same way, with no signal-strength differentiation. This is exactly what Cosign wants to fix: ensuring you only spend time with people you should actually meet, rather than sifting through mountains of connection requests yourself.

item.title: Ready-made data connectors fail over 40% of the time, forcing OpenAI to build its own pipeline
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-31-latentspace-现成数据接口错误率超40-逼得openai自建数据管道/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-31-latentspace-现成数据接口错误率超40-逼得openai自建数据管道/
item.description: Testing revealed error rates exceeding 40% on well-known MCP data connectors, pushing OpenAI to abandon third-party integration and build proprietary data pipelines as a core competitive advantage for its financial products.
item.content:encoded:
Testing revealed error rates exceeding 40% on well-known MCP data connectors, pushing OpenAI to abandon third-party integration and build proprietary data pipelines as a core competitive advantage for its financial products.

This episode reveals an overlooked trap in enterprise AI products: third-party connectors marketed as ready-made often have error rates far higher than expected.

1:20 Financial products work as consumer ChatGPT plus enterprise layer
ChatGPT for Financial Services is not a new model. It layers industry-specific capabilities—templates, data sources like S&P—on top of the same ChatGPT, co-designed with Morgan Stanley and Evercore. Joseph emphasizes this layering pattern repeatedly: real product value lives in the enterprise customization, not in advancing the base model.

3:45 Codex adoption in finance jumped from 0 to 90%
Internal metrics show Codex adoption among software engineers rose steadily, but adoption in finance, legal, and sales stayed near zero—until Codex shipped a desktop app. Then adoption jumped to 90%. The bottleneck was never capability; it was making capability usable through a product interface.

6:08 Third-party data connectors have over 40% error rates; build them yourself
The team wanted to use existing MCP connectors to ingest financial data. On the surface, it's cheaper—customers already own licenses and MCP subscriptions, so asking for a separate data-integration fee feels wrong. Testing proved otherwise: some well-known MCP connectors had error rates above 40%. The team pulled that work in-house, absorbing the cost. The payoff came in customer feedback, where data quality was the most-mentioned strength.

8:40 Codex gives you 80%; the last 20% is the whole game
Joseph describes his team as operating like a startup built on OpenAI technology. Codex ships with memory, skills, and persistence—enough to get a financial product 80% usable. But wrapping Codex directly as a financial product would fail. That missing 20%—data, UI, integration—is the deciding factor. He sees this pattern (ChatGPT infrastructure plus proprietary secret sauce: data, UI, integration) spawning billion-dollar businesses.

12:00 Design model permissions like onboarding a new employee
How should next-gen agents be governed? Forget new safety frameworks. Reuse what human organizations already do: graduated trust. Like Google's readability credential—new engineers can't submit code in certain languages until they prove they know the codebase—models should have read/write tiers. Go further: borrow the investment-banking hierarchy (analyst, associate, VP, managing director) where every level reviews the next one's work. This mechanism for handling human error scales directly to models.

14:00 The killer isn't factual errors anymore—it's bad taste
Joseph separates two error classes: factual error (cite the wrong number, your whole conclusion collapses, you lose your job) and taste error (ugly slide colors, sloppy layout—non-fatal but damaging to how your work lands). He observes hallucination was a frequent word in 2022–23. Almost never mentioned now. Progress on factual errors is real. Subjective judgment—taste—is what comes next.

16:45 Teach aesthetic judgment through pairwise human comparison
How do you train taste? The answer is strikingly simple: show people two slides, ask which is better, feed the pairwise preference signal into a reward model. This is early-stage RLHF—exactly how it started—which the field neglected while chasing verifiable rewards like "does the code compile?" Here's what surprised Joseph: humans size up a slide's aesthetics in seconds. Let models judge instead, and they burn massive reasoning overhead and still get it wrong. For taste, humans still outscore models.

23:50 Finance benchmarks are broken at scale
Knowledge-work evaluations hit saturation with Astra. The parts still unsaturated are the ones that are broken. The team stopped reporting this metric entirely. There's a pattern internally: score goes up, no one asks questions; score doesn't move, dig into it. GPT-6 didn't shift on some finance evals. Investigation revealed the answer keys were wrong, prompts weren't crisp—the problem was the test, not the model. The team is now building new benchmarks that can predict whether a given job can actually be automated.

item.title: Anthropic's $80 billion loss is accounting fiction; actual cash burn under $10 billion
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-allin-anthropic800亿美元亏损是假账-实际烧钱不到100亿/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-allin-anthropic800亿美元亏损是假账-实际烧钱不到100亿/
item.description: The $80 billion loss stems from convertible notes issued to Amazon and other infrastructure partners—as the company's valuation rises, these notes generate larger accounting losses on the income statement, but the cash never actually left. Total actual cash burned is only $9–10 billion.
item.content:encoded:
The $80 billion loss stems from convertible notes issued to Amazon and other infrastructure partners—as the company's valuation rises, these notes generate larger accounting losses on the income statement, but the cash never actually left. Total actual cash burned is only $9–10 billion.

Clarify the most controversial figures in Anthropic's S-1 filing, plus hard information about compute dependence, AI debt's impact on the Treasury market, and the RSI roadmap dispute that only surfaces in the later sections.

3:01 Anthropic's S-1 targets $1.5–2 trillion valuation
The filing shows Anthropic hit $16.3 billion revenue in H1 2026, up 14x year-over-year, with Q2 alone at $11.6 billion—a 30x surge from the prior five quarters. The company aims to raise $100 billion through IPO at a valuation target of $1.5–2 trillion, which if successful would surpass SpaceX as the largest IPO in history. Sacks directly calls it one of capitalism's greatest businesses.

7:16 $80 billion accounting loss, not real loss
Media long pointed to this loss to claim Anthropic is a cash-burning story, but the filing shows it stems from convertible notes issued to infrastructure partners like Amazon—as company valuation rises, these notes trigger larger accounting losses on the P&L, yet no cash actually leaves. Sacks points out Anthropic raised roughly $110 billion total with actual cash burn of only $9–10 billion, while $100 billion sits on the balance sheet—a company of extreme capital efficiency.

13:40 $1 of Nvidia spending becomes $18 in revenue
Freeberg maps profit distribution across the entire AI stack: Nvidia spends $1 to make a chip and sells it for $4, with 75% gross margin; compute companies amortize chips over five years and achieve 83% gross margin; Anthropic discloses incremental gross margin above 85%. Chain it together and $1 of Nvidia spending becomes $18 in revenue—nearly every link in the chain is profitable, proving AI creates real productive value, not just capital burn.

18:47 Compute is the only real fear in the filing
Chamath had the team count word frequency in risk factors, and they overwhelmingly point to compute—data centers, power grids, electricity, chips rank first, with regulation second; the company barely mentions customer churn or employee attrition. He draws a political inference: if Democrats want to engineer recession before 2028, the most efficient lever is blocking power and data center approvals; if Republicans want to win, they must deliver on power and data centers.

30:08 Cash is larger than expected; Chamath walks back forecast
Chamath previously predicted Anthropic would need $200–250 billion in cash reserves and a $1 trillion valuation. But reading the filing, he found the company already held $125 billion in cash by June with total net cash burn of only $9–10 billion—far more cushion than he'd forecast. So he revised: the company needs only $80–120 billion more, and IPO pricing likely lands between $1.3–1.7 trillion, with $1.5 trillion as midpoint.

32:12 AI's top seven firms' debt now equals 30% of Treasury issuance
Chamath's deeper concern isn't whether Anthropic's business works, but that the entire AI complex now owes the market $340–400 billion, and by year-end 2027, these companies will need to raise capital equal to 30% of concurrent US Treasury issuance. This means AI is now competing with the US government for capital markets, and if competition raises borrowing costs, risk propagates through the entire industry chain—he says this is a dynamic he's only seen in financial crises over the past 15–20 years.

43:40 Anthropic publicly calls for restraint while pursuing recursive self-improvement
Sacks notes Anthropic publicly urges the industry to decelerate while pushing recursive self-improvement (RSI) more aggressively than any company—using its own models to discover algorithm improvements and compute multipliers, the key to achieving 10x cost efficiency versus peers. In an August blog, Anthropic disclosed 26% of model iteration tasks already use RSI. Sacks suggests the public deceleration letter reads like a pre-written liability waiver—if RSI goes wrong, they can claim others refused to cooperate.

1:01:57 Google erased $500 billion in market value overnight
Google's stock shed roughly $500 billion the day after earnings as search ads disappointed for two straight quarters—search volume is climbing but click-through rates lagged. Cloud revenue doubled year-over-year to $30.7 billion, with operating profit soaring from $35 billion prior-year to over $110 billion. More troubling: a post with 5 million views accused Google of quietly abandoning the Vickrey auction mechanism, systematically overcharging advertisers. Sacks counters that search revenue actually grew 12% year-over-year from $56 billion to $63 billion; cloud just grew faster, compressing search's share below 50%.

item.title: Without non-competes, advisors can leave anytime, yet this trillion-dollar wealth manager has the industry's lowest churn
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-mastersinbiz-没有竞业协议-顾问随时能走-这家万亿资管公司流失率却最低/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-mastersinbiz-没有竞业协议-顾问随时能走-这家万亿资管公司流失率却最低/
item.description: LPL's advisors are independent contractors with no non-competes, free to leave anytime. LPL even helps them transfer client data when they go. This forces LPL to re-earn their trust every day, resulting in churn far lower than the industry's 5%.
item.content:encoded:
LPL's advisors are independent contractors with no non-competes, free to leave anytime. LPL even helps them transfer client data when they go. This forces LPL to re-earn their trust every day, resulting in churn far lower than the industry's 5%.

This episode uses concrete numbers to explain how a platform managing $2.6 trillion in assets keeps advisors, deploys AI, and executes M&A—grounded in case details with high information density.

12:20 Robo-advisors didn't actually eliminate human advisors
In the mid-2010s, the wealth-management industry feared robo-advisors would eliminate jobs for human advisors. Steinmeier recalls genuinely fearing this during his time at UBS. Instead, the price and performance transparency robo-advisors introduced actually raised client expectations for all advisors—the combination of technology and people proved better than either alone. LPL's example: by using robotic tools to drive account-opening costs from thousands of dollars down to a few, LPL could afford to eliminate account minimums.

29:40 Acquisitions aim to avoid homogenization, not just scale
LPL acquired Commonwealth for $2.7 billion, adding to earlier deals like Atria, rapidly scaling up. But Steinmeier stressed the real risk isn't affordability—it's whether acquired companies get homogenized afterward. Backend functions like account setup, account transfers, and core technology can consolidate, but acquired firms' response patterns to advisors and service experience must be deliberately preserved and isolated. He summarizes this approach as ‘growing while feeling small’.

35:48 Despite its scale, LPL functions as a small company
Steinmeier uses ‘small company that's big’ to describe LPL's current state: as scale grew, so did processes, discipline, and structure, but he doesn't want the company to lose its human touch. He says this is the real strategy behind recent acquisitions—how to gain scale and investment capacity without letting the organization homogenize into a sprawling machine.

37:50 Advisors spend 70% of time on processes, not clients
LPL measured advisor time at the office: only 30% goes to actual client advice, the remaining 70% to process work—meeting prep, plan updates, tax optimization. Steinmeier says AI investment's core goal is compressing that 70%: starting with tools for meeting notes and note-taking, then expanding to account automation and portfolio construction. This ratio is LPL's baseline for measuring AI value, and why it chose to build its own technology stack rather than patch together third-party tools.

39:52 AI deployment splits into three layers: advisors, company, engineers
LPL splits AI applications into three categories: first, advisor-office workflows—auto-populating account forms, submitting, then human review; second, internal company workflows like compliance checks and fund transfers (representing 80% of that 70% process time); third, making ~3,000 internal developers more efficient at code. Separate investment tracks because automation depth and risk tolerance differ completely across categories—one toolkit can't address all three.

42:59 Without non-competes, LPL helps departing advisors take their clients
LPL's advisors are all independent contractors—no non-compete clauses in their contracts, free to move their book anytime. Counterintuitively, when advisors do leave, LPL doesn't try to retain their clients like some firms do; instead it helps them transfer client data along. Steinmeier says this forces LPL to re-earn advisor trust every day rather than rely on contract lock-in. The result: industry churn runs ~5%, LPL's sits at 1.5%.

47:02 Portfolio allocation shifts from 60-40 to 40-30-30 structure
LPL's research team observed traditional 60-40 stock-bond portfolios evolving toward 40% stocks, 30% bonds, 30% alternatives (private equity, private credit, uncorrelated assets). Steinmeier supports lowering the bar to access alternatives—even pushing legislation to let 401(k) plans hold them—but admits the industry hasn't reached consensus on where to set the asset-size minimum.

52:06 In ten years, advisor time shifts to 70% with clients, 30% on process
Steinmeier predicts the next decade will flip today's 30%-70% ratio: advisors spend 70% on client service, 30% on backend. More controversially, he foresees only a handful of peer wealth platforms surviving—those building their own technology, holding their own clearing capability, operating their own advisor workstations and investment tools, and sharing unified data with AI agents. Platforms merely stitching together third-party tools will be eliminated.

item.title: AI agents now drive 70% of new database growth, not human engineers
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-ycsp-数据库公司七成新增用量来自ai代理-不是人类工程师/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-ycsp-数据库公司七成新增用量来自ai代理-不是人类工程师/
item.description: People across industries no longer need to convince engineers to get started: AI lets people who understand business build complex systems directly, and there's currently no ceiling on the growth of this new builder cohort.
item.content:encoded:
People across industries no longer need to convince engineers to get started: AI lets people who understand business build complex systems directly, and there's currently no ceiling on the growth of this new builder cohort.

One infrastructure company lived through three complete transitions—dashboard to API to code-first—providing empirical evidence of how AI is reshaping who can be an entrepreneur.

1:05 In one year, managed databases grew from 8 million to 50 million
Superbase registered users rose from roughly 3 million a year ago to 13 million; over 1 million new databases are created weekly; total managed databases approach 50 million (up from 8 million a year ago); revenue is projected to grow 4x this year. The driver isn't just that AI helps software engineers write code faster—the real inflection point is that people without engineering backgrounds can now build directly on Superbase for the first time.

4:14 Unusual growth curve: conversion metrics improved during explosive user scaling
Usually when user counts surge, activation and conversion metrics dilute and decline—it's an almost-universal law in product growth. But this year all of Superbase's related metrics rose simultaneously, because models became strong enough that people who couldn't write code could now build it. The old investor claim that product-led growth tops out at some revenue threshold and must shift to sales-driven growth has not held true as of this year.

14:34 Scaling to 1.2 billion monthly database creations is uncharted territory for the industry
Paul did arithmetic using ChatGPT's 1.2 billion weekly active users: if each user wanted to build something once a month, that's 1.2 billion databases/month—a scale the database industry has never had to handle. The company acquired Terso (compatible with Postgres and SQLite), launched lightweight Superbase Spark, positioned as ‘from prototype to petabytes’, and maintains both a multi-tenant architecture that scales to petabytes and an architecture for lightweight starter scenarios.

17:36 Code at home: engineers were convinced, not mandated
The company has no AI usage policy—employees use whatever tools they want. The result: 10% of engineers writing 80% of code using AI grew to 60% of engineers doing the same within six months—not through force, but because engineers were gradually convinced by the model's actual output quality. As AI-generated code increased, the team also massively increased the test volume they wrote to verify correctness—the same pattern shows up at other YC companies like Blacksmith and UbiCloud.

20:42 Three transitions shaped the product: dashboard, API, then code-first
Each transition had a concrete trigger. The first came when software engineers themselves found databases too hard to use, so they built a dashboard (like Airtable) on top of Postgres. The second came in 2021 when a customer's bulk-database request forced out an API, just as AI site-builders like Bolt and Lovable exploded in 2024. The third happened this year: the team noticed almost no one was accessing the dashboard anymore, so they rebuilt the CLI and entire product as ‘infrastructure as code’, naturally matching how agents work.

30:57 Winning agents takes two phases: selection, then preventing switching
Superbase rewrote error messages designed for humans—the ‘HTTP 500’ style—to tell agents directly how to fix the problem and which docs to read. Winning the AI-tools business has two steps: first, get selected as the default database, then when an agent gets stuck (and all agents eventually get stuck), make sure it doesn't switch to a different tool. Give it self-healing capabilities. Rewriting product details specifically for agents rather than humans now takes up significant engineering effort.

33:07 Personal knowledge bases need retrieval structure, not just a bigger context window
GBrain's builders found that no context window is large enough—100k tokens ≈ three Harry Potter books, but getting an agent to pull exactly the right three books when answering a question is hard. So they used Postgres's pgvector to build a retrieval system, organizing unstructured data into a graph structure directly in the database, then ran automated roles like Cappy 24/7 in eval loops, continuously testing and improving retrieval accuracy—essentially a very primitive recursive self-improvement loop for one specific task.

43:32 Vertical SaaS fundraising is hard; small teams hit high margins with AI
The market has an anomaly: vertical SaaS companies with $5–10 million annual revenue struggle to raise Series A (this was a stable threshold nine to twelve months ago), but horizontal and AI-related projects sail through. Meanwhile, a 15-person team can hit $25–50 million in annual revenue, $2 million in ARR per person, and 50% margins—no longer needing a huge funding round to hire bodies. ‘Didn't raise funding’ went from a source of embarrassment to something worth envying.

item.title: Open-Weight Models Framed as Cyber Weapons Were Released; the World Didn't Collapse
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-interconnects-被渲染成网络武器的开源模型发布后-世界并没有崩溃/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-interconnects-被渲染成网络武器的开源模型发布后-世界并没有崩溃/
item.description: Open-weight models crossed the putative cyber-weapon threshold over a month ago with no evidence of step-change disaster, but the author concedes this still constitutes a costly, forced industry upgrade.
item.content:encoded:
Open-weight models crossed the putative cyber-weapon threshold over a month ago with no evidence of step-change disaster, but the author concedes this still constitutes a costly, forced industry upgrade.

The author's willingness to put his predictions from weeks ago on the line for reality-testing is more honest than most post-hoc retrospectives.

1:20 Models that crossed the threshold haven't triggered the predicted disaster
Claude Mythos was initially framed as a potential catastrophe if weights leaked. In reality, GLM-5.3 is what crossed that capability threshold—and its open weights have been publicly available for over a month with almost no public evidence of corresponding-scale destruction. The author speculates that even if Claude Mythos had been accidentally leaked as open weights, the world would likely remain essentially intact: network-security incidents would increase noticeably and cause real harm, but this would be an acceleration rather than a step-change.

2:10 A falsifiable prediction is being falsified by real-world evidence
The author frames the open-weight catastrophe narrative as a testable claim: open-weight models will cause unprecedented, infrastructure-paralyzing harm at scale. By his current evidence, this prediction is being falsified—which is why he's writing this reflection. After years of theoretical debate about open-weight risks, reality is finally providing answers instead of endless hypothesis-based argument.

3:00 Alarmist framing penetrated government-level threat assessment
To show the catastrophe narrative wasn't his misreading, the author cites specific statements: Rob Wiblin saying leaked weights would be ‘an actual disaster’; Anthropic's Project Glasswing warning of serious economic, public-safety, and national-security consequences. The point isn't whether those exact words appeared, but how the public and federal government received this language—the narrative genuinely crystallized into a cyber-weapon story in policy circles.

4:50 A single exploit chain remains incomplete without multiple conditions aligning
Epoch AI demonstrated GLM-5.3's capability to find and chain exploits; the public Firefox case illustrates why network harm requires multiple prerequisites: they built a webpage, Firefox users merely visited it, and attackers could steal files from their computers. But this was only one link in the attack chain—the attacker still needed to actually seed that webpage into places victims would visit, a multi-stage, multi-actor process. Finding a vulnerability is not the same as causing harm.

6:10 ‘Fine’understates the disruption if you didn't anticipate upheaval
The author acknowledges his prior use of ‘fine’ was imprecise. The more accurate framing: this will force a costly, industry-wide upgrade. The software industry must fundamentally change how it operates alongside AI, at significant expense and with substantial remediation work. If you already expected disruption, ‘fine’ is apt; if you saw no warning signs of a transition period, the term underestimates what's coming.

6:50 Open-weight models are tilting the offense-defense balance toward defenders
The author's core finding: open-weight models currently favor defensive adoption over offensive exploitation. The reasoning: attackers generally command fewer resources than enterprises. Enterprises will likely patch vulnerabilities faster using open models than attackers can weaponize them. The critical variable he's now watching is whether adversaries will inflict material physical harm within the US and its allies. Current evidence shows they're likely already conducting large-scale covert data theft with these tools, but no evidence yet that anyone is bringing full capability to bear against public institutions for mass destruction.

8:00 Threat actors operate as business enterprises, not as pure saboteurs
The author cites a tweet that captures this: stop imagining threat actors as willing to break anything to penetrate a system; think of them as having fixed business processes. Bakeries don't switch to making dog food because kibble runs short. ClickFix operators won't suddenly abandon their playbook to learn zero-day coding from scratch. Those actively using these exploits are exactly those already in the exploitation business—not a coincidence, but a predictable outcome of threat-actor economics.

9:20 Most discovered exploits were likely found by closed-model systems, not open weights
The author makes a deliberate but high-uncertainty prediction: the majority of presently-documented vulnerabilities probably originated from closed-model discovery, not open-weight models. This judgment hinges on how open models actually get deployed near-term. Today's open-weight model serving costs remain elevated, inherently limiting attackers' ability to run vulnerability-discovery campaigns at scale.

item.title: The biographer of power's corruption: America can't build things because it overcorrected
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-dwarkesh-写权力如何腐化人的传记作家说-美国建不成东西-是矫枉过正/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-dwarkesh-写权力如何腐化人的传记作家说-美国建不成东西-是矫枉过正/
item.description: He says today's environmental reviews, community committees, and lawsuits are no fewer obstacles than in Moses's era; what's truly scarce is someone willing to find workarounds and get things done despite all resistance.
item.content:encoded:
He says today's environmental reviews, community committees, and lawsuits are no fewer obstacles than in Moses's era; what's truly scarce is someone willing to find workarounds and get things done despite all resistance.

Core value lies in Moses's character transformation and the question of why construction became harder; sections on writing methods and digital archives have lower information density and can be skipped.

9:02 America's building paralysis stems from overcorrecting Moses-era obstacles
Moses forced his way around landowner opposition to build Jones Beach, yet today's Second Avenue Subway took nearly 50 years to open 1.5 miles at $4 billion, and California's high-speed rail burned through $15 billion without completing a single mile. Caro argues these are the costs of safety mechanisms added to prevent another Moses; they block everyone, not just the ruthless. America now needs some ‘Moses’ energy—but without his disregard for public opinion.

16:57 Idealists turn ruthless when repeated obstacles force adaptation
Moses started as a true idealist: he studied civil service reform to make promotion merit-based, not political, and wanted to open Long Island beaches to the poor. But building the Cross Bronx Expressway, he refused compromise even when offered to shift two blocks south and reduce displacements from tens of thousands to hundreds. He bulldozed through anyway; when completed, it became the world's longest traffic jam, displacing thousands without relocation. Caro notes this wasn't sudden moral collapse but gradual learning: after enough failures, ruthlessness becomes pragmatic.

20:30 When power vanishes, the phone stops ringing
At Moses's peak influence, secretaries interrupted Caro's interviews bearing stacks of callers requesting favors. Years later, when Moses had lost power, Caro noticed no calls arrived after they finished talking—nobody needed him anymore. More dramatically, in 1962 Moses tried his usual tactic: threatening to resign unless Rockefeller obeyed. Rockefeller's answer: ‘I regret to accept it’—the threat that had worked on every previous mayor and governor simply failed.

26:05 Destroying opponents became Moses's tool as resistance hardened
Bronx politician Henry Epstein opposed the Cross Bronx route and proposed shifting two blocks south to cut displacements from tens of thousands to a few hundred. Instead of reconsidering, Moses destroyed Epstein by spreading rumors about an affair. Caro shows this became Moses's pattern: find someone blocking you, uncover their weakness—infidelity, corruption, any leverage—and deploy it without hesitation. This ruthlessness was Moses's self-taught survival law, born from years of failed attempts at compromise.

29:50 Depression-era cheap labor built faster and more beautiful
Moses accomplished so much partly because the Great Depression flooded the market with desperate architects he could hire cheaply and fire at will. Caro notes a paradox: early 20th-century buildings like Grand Central Terminal were more beautiful than later ones, also because labor was cheaper—developers could afford to hire craftsmen to carve decorative stonework on rooftops nobody would see. Scarcity of money paradoxically enabled abundance of beauty.

37:00 Kennedy lacked Johnson's obsession with remaking America
When Dwarkesh asked whether civil rights and anti-poverty legislation would have passed sooner if Kennedy had won without needing Johnson as vice president, Caro said no. Kennedy was charming and skilled diplomatically, but lacked Johnson's drive to fundamentally transform America. Johnson's obsession stemmed from youth teaching poor children in Cotulla—it fueled his later education and anti-poverty laws. Caro admits he still doesn't understand why Johnson kept escalating Vietnam; that mystery will be his next book.

45:57 Cutting 350,000 words meant losing entire lives from the record
Caro submitted The Power Broker at 1.05 million words; fitting one volume required cutting to roughly 700 pages—350,000 words gone. His editor Bob Gottlieb said ‘I deleted some of the best things I've ever read.’ Among the cut material were detailed accounts of figures like Sam Rayburn, who actually controlled the House and passed countless Roosevelt bills, yet has no proper biography. Caro donated his files to the New-York Historical Society at reduced cost so future researchers could access this unpublished material.

52:02 The frontier's true cost was grinding isolation, not violence
Western films never captured the real loneliness of hill country: Johnson's ancestors moved to the Texas frontier where Indian raids were possible, but the grinding agony was daily life without neighbors. Caro's chapter on Johnson's mother describes her walking uphill and seeing only more hills. Elderly women he interviewed would say ‘22 miles from Austin you'd see a cattle pen; another 22 miles before you got to our place’—no other households between. Caro admits this frontier isolation shaped himself: he stopped answering his phone decades ago, a habit that echoed through his entire social life.

item.title: Going long on compute takes more than chips: Silicon Valley's inside joke about structural shorts
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-asianometry-想做多算力-光囤芯片不够-不借钱加仓就是-结构性做空/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-asianometry-想做多算力-光囤芯片不够-不借钱加仓就是-结构性做空/
item.description: Someone explained to the author that buying compute with equity alone isn't truly ‘going long’—you need debt leverage on chips too, or you're ‘structurally short’. It's a Silicon Valley inside joke.
item.content:encoded:
Someone explained to the author that buying compute with equity alone isn't truly ‘going long’—you need debt leverage on chips too, or you're ‘structurally short’. It's a Silicon Valley inside joke.

To understand Silicon Valley insiders' firsthand take on the AI compute arms race, cooling valuations, and the real cash flow picture at startups. This episode is more direct than earnings calls but leans toward on-the-ground anecdotes rather than hard data.

2:07 Open Compute has overshadowed the legacy semiconductor trade show
Semicon West, which alternated between San Francisco and Arizona, is holding its last SF edition; the next moves to Arizona in March 2027. It's losing to OCP Global Summit, which dominates the same week with focus on inference-era infrastructure (cooling, networking). The author expects Semicon to eventually relocate to Texas, reflecting the geographic shift of US chip manufacturing away from Silicon Valley toward inland states.

4:07 Anthropic's $16 billion revenue fails to satisfy markets
During the author's visit, the Financial Times reported Anthropic's financials: $16 billion annualized revenue with excellent margins—numbers any industry would celebrate. Yet markets deemed it insufficient; AI stocks pivoted on the news. It's a snapshot of the disconnect between builders inside the conference and financial markets outside, anxious enough to stretch 2027 overcapacity worries into questions about whether 2028 demand can hold up.

5:16 Equipment capex forecasts hide a textbook bullwhip effect
Lam Research raised 2026 wafer fab equipment capex guidance from $140 billion to $150 billion and projects 2027 spending above $200 billion. Goldman Sachs forecasts $218 billion for 2027 and $281 billion for 2028. Yet at the same event, the author hears rumors that equipment suppliers are quietly freezing hires. Demand signals amplifying upstream while hiring throttles at the source: textbook bullwhip effect.

7:23 The jagged edge explains why startups must build custom models
Silicon Valley entrepreneurs repeatedly invoke ‘jagged edge’ to explain custom model development: today's large language models excel at some tasks while failing unpredictably at others, and the boundary is hard to predict. Step off the ‘golden path’ of well-trained tasks and performance cliffs. The author notes the same term describes Chinese open-source models—dominant in niche domains but with equally stark weak spots.

8:25 Not leveraging debt on chips is ‘structurally short’—a Silicon Valley inside joke
Smart investors believe every additional gigawatt of compute grows more valuable, so many prefer equity financing over debt to buy chips; debt default is a common company killer. But others push back: if equity-only chip acquisition can't match a rival's speed, raw compute scale crushes you anyway. Real ‘going long’ isn't just raising capital to buy chips—it's borrowing to add leverage on top and buy more. Anything else is ‘structurally shorting’ yourself. It's a running inside joke.

9:26 Startups burn through subscription subsidies to stay alive
Semianalysis research shows a $200/month Claude or ChatGPT subscription yields $2,000–$14,000 in equivalent API value. Cash-strapped startups accumulate multiple subscriptions, burning hard at token resets. Some route entire customer-facing products through these subsidized subscription tokens. The author sees this as obviously unsustainable, economically deformed business models masquerading as real companies.

11:30 AI subscription subsidies mimic the rideshare wars of 2015–16
The author recalls 2016 leaked Uber financials showing customers paid only 41% of actual trip costs—sometimes including extreme driver subsidies in China (three times the fare per ride). Today's AI subscription subsidies aren't yet that aggressive. But OpenAI's premium Pro 500+ tier and startup migration toward native API pricing show markets adjusting. Startups are rebuilding unit economics around true API costs and exploring load-balancing across multiple models.

13:34 Massive math API spending might fund automated research loops
OpenAI and Anthropic spent roughly $6.5 million in API calls on Navier-Stokes proofs and similar math problems. Even with ample compute, the scale seems extreme for a blog post. One theory: the spend primes Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). Train models to reliably prove or disprove a hypothesis, then automate a sweep across human-generated hypotheses, verify them, and feed results back into training. By this logic, math spending isn't marketing but a cornerstone of coming R&D.

item.title: Small Law Firms Could Reach Billion-Dollar Revenues With AI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-a16z-小型律所靠ai也能做到十亿美元生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-a16z-小型律所靠ai也能做到十亿美元生意/
item.description: The bottleneck for plaintiff lawyers has never been client supply—it's labor. A Los Angeles law firm used AI to increase clients per attorney from 100 to 500, revealing the true market for legal AI.
item.content:encoded:
The bottleneck for plaintiff lawyers has never been client supply—it's labor. A Los Angeles law firm used AI to increase clients per attorney from 100 to 500, revealing the true market for legal AI.

Essential for founders and investors seeking to understand how AI can reshape professional services economics; no legal background required to follow.

3:03 Contingency fees prove result-based pricing works in professional services
Plaintiff law has charged on contingency—a percentage of the settlement—since its inception, because ordinary people cannot afford the blank-check hourly legal fees. Jay argues this model is the template for results-based pricing, and fields like corporate counsel and immigration law that still charge hourly would benefit from adopting it.

8:11 96% of employment cases are rejected because the math doesn't work
A call comes in, and the lawyer spends 30 to 45 minutes screening it, then 10 hours on legal research and assessing whether there's a viable cause of action. Often they discover the case wouldn't generate even $5,000 in revenue—less than the cost to pursue it. Jay explains this is precisely why 96% of employment and labor cases are rejected for representation: it's not that people lack valid claims, but that the economics don't pencil out.

14:25 A Los Angeles firm multiplied clients per attorney fivefold with AI
Jay describes how one LA law firm pushed Eve—the AI—to its limits: handling intake calls, qualification screening, case routing between attorneys and paralegals, and settlement strategy recommendations. The result: clients per attorney jumped from 100 to 500. This wasn't layoffs; it was the same people earning multiples more.

16:26 Low software spending in plaintiff law reflects labor bottleneck, not market size
Alex highlights an error VCs have made for years: plaintiff firms historically had minimal software spending—just phones, email, maybe no Microsoft Office—since adversaries don't collaborate on documents. But this doesn't mean the market is small. The industry generates hundreds of billions in annual settlements; it's simply constrained by labor capacity. The software opportunity is actually an undervalued shadow labor market.

21:36 A thousand Einsteins couldn't immediately succeed at a law firm they don't know
Jay argues that even a thousand Einsteins parachuting into a law firm would not immediately be productive, because critical information simply isn't available online. Less than 1% of cases ever produce a published decision—most settle privately before filing. Knowing how to counter tactics from insurance companies comes from informal knowledge shared among lawyers. That's what Eve provides: not just a smarter model, but access to practitioner expertise.

34:05 Agents will handle routine disputes, leaving lawyers to focus on courtroom work
Jay predicts the industry will shift toward automated dispute resolution (ADR), where routine back-and-forth communication in many cases becomes agent-to-agent negotiation. Historically, taking a case to trial shut down the entire firm's operations for prep work. Now that Eve handles procedural work, some clients are actually willing to invest more time in actual courtroom advocacy rather than pushing everything toward quick settlement.

36:05 Small law firms can reach billion-dollar revenues through specialization and AI
Alex poses a question: if clients per attorney jumped from 100 to 500, why couldn't it reach 5,000—and if so, why should small firms limit themselves to a single state? Jay outlines two diverging paths: one where firms continue specializing as they did 30 years ago, narrowing toward specific injury types like soft-tissue damage and relying on reputation rather than advertising. The other: large firms using Eve to accelerate acquisition and consolidation of smaller practices.

50:49 Insurance companies' delay tactics don't work when agents respond in real time
A partner firm discovered that opposing insurers typically timed discovery requests for the day before Thanksgiving, betting the other side would be on holiday and unable to process them carefully. The firm deployed an agent that responded the same day, catching the insurer unprepared. Jay observes that this kind of tactical back-and-forth is becoming agent-versus-agent competition.

item.title: Anthropic's $80 Billion 'Loss' Is Just an Accounting Illusion
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-sharptech-anthropic的800亿美元-亏损-只是一场会计幻觉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-sharptech-anthropic的800亿美元-亏损-只是一场会计幻觉/
item.description: The money is a paper loss from Amazon's convertible loan being repriced as valuation changes—no cash outflow; what's truly concerning is that training costs are growing faster than service costs and remain completely outside the company's control.
item.content:encoded:
The money is a paper loss from Amazon's convertible loan being repriced as valuation changes—no cash outflow; what's truly concerning is that training costs are growing faster than service costs and remain completely outside the company's control.

Anthropic has disclosed complete financial details for the first time, allowing you to distinguish real costs from accounting artifacts in the AI spending race—critical for judging the pace of capital expenditure across the entire industry.

8:22 Training costs exceed service revenue growth and escape management control
The S1 filing shows Anthropic's H1 revenue surged while R&D—specifically training—expenditure grew faster than service costs. The reason: maintaining model leadership requires continuous model training, and how much to spend and when to spend it are entirely beyond the company's control. This is ongoing operational cost, not a one-time capital investment that can be managed once a problem is solved. Thompson points out that this collapses the distance between "limiting frontier speed for safety" and the reality of "burning money to survive".

12:26 Revenue returned to cloud platforms should count as cost of sales
About half of Anthropic's revenue flows through AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, but roughly 37 percent is paid back to these platforms. The company counts the full amount as revenue and records the payments back as a sales and marketing expense rather than cost of goods sold. Thompson argues this portion should properly count as cost of revenue, which would significantly compress the company's reported gross margins.

16:31 The $80 billion loss is mark-to-market repricing, not cash outflow
Early reports claimed Anthropic lost $80 billion in H1, which sounds catastrophic. Thompson explains this is not cash out the door. Amazon's investment took the form of a convertible loan, and every time Anthropic raises at a new valuation, the loan is repriced and the difference is recorded as a paper loss. The same money surfaces on Amazon's financial statements as gain on investment—it's an accounting identity on opposite sides of a ledger, not cash destruction.

19:33 Shareholder dilution is written into the equity structure itself
A cited tweet traces how large companies finance: first free cash flow, then debt, now equity dilution. Anthropic's situation is extreme: Amazon, Google, and Broadcom hold agreements to convert stakes into equity over time. Every valuation increase forces a new dilution round, and the agreements actually require issuing additional shares if the stock price crosses certain thresholds—dilution is baked into the company structure itself.

43:25 An AI bubble exists only if revenue cannot cover capex
Craig Moffett offers a simplified test: ignore the noise of companies trading revenue with each other along the value chain, and look only at the total revenue flowing into the system—is it enough to cover the capex required to build out that chain? Thompson agrees with this framework and notes that even Anthropic's rapid revenue growth remains far short of covering industry-wide capex, which is being deployed for years ahead. Real victory depends on whether revenue growth can accelerate further.

45:30 Cloud vendors alone have the cash to bridge the AI capex gap
Thompson argues that whoever has the thickest cash flow, strongest borrowing capacity, and strongest ability to issue equity becomes the bridge across the AI capex chasm: Google, Amazon, and Microsoft. Nvidia, in reverse, provides financial backing to emerging cloud competitors—essentially hedging against the risk that "the entire industry runs out of money before revenue catches up to costs." This mirrors the path history took with railroad booms and collapses.

58:03 Training costs force Meta to invest ruthlessly in Muse platform
Thompson wrote the S1 analysis showing training costs as the primary, uncontrollable cost center, then analyzed Meta's earnings report and realized it illuminated Meta's massive Muse spending. To become the "aggregator of aggregators" in the AI era—the ultimate user-facing layer—you must control your own models, which means you must spend heavily on training. This logic chain is indivisible; opposing Muse funding is really opposing the pursuit of Muse itself.

1:08:19 Meta's push for engagement indirectly drives Netflix viewers away
Thompson surfaces a rare angle: Meta's massive AI investment pressure creates enormous investor expectations for returns, so Meta maximizes engagement in Reels and the feed—flooding users with short video and ads to keep them addicted. This directly competes for time users would otherwise spend on Netflix, making Netflix an indirect victim of the capital demands imposed by AI spending.

item.title: Kids Demanding iPhones Are Really After Inclusion
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-raisinggh-孩子吵着要iphone-其实要的是不被排除在外/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-30-raisinggh-孩子吵着要iphone-其实要的是不被排除在外/
item.description: Sociologist Stacy Kim says jealousy itself is a neutral signal: you only envy people close enough to you, people you genuinely care about. Learn to stop watching the other person and instead ask about the feeling itself—that's how you turn jealousy into action.
item.content:encoded:
Sociologist Stacy Kim says jealousy itself is a neutral signal: you only envy people close enough to you, people you genuinely care about. Learn to stop watching the other person and instead ask about the feeling itself—that's how you turn jealousy into action.

Suitable for parents wanting to understand the psychology of jealousy and how to respond well when children express admiration toward classmates. Contains two ad breaks you can skip.

1:00 Korean has two jealousy words, English has one
Kim discovered that moving between Korea and the US revealed a crucial difference: Korean has two words for jealousy—시기 (Shigi) for malicious envy, rarely spoken aloud, and 부러워/푸러워 (Puro) meaning roughly ‘I also want to be like you’, which actually opens conversation and invites a response like ‘you can do it too’. English, and most English-speaking cultures, have only one word for jealousy, bound by association to ‘the seven deadly sins,’ which makes Americans reluctant to discuss it openly. German, Dutch, Russian, Thai, and Chinese all have two words for jealousy. Spanish and English are rare exceptions with only one.

7:17 The person you envy must be someone you can reach
Kim identifies a rule about who triggers envy: an orchestra cellist doesn't envy Yo-Yo Ma but admires him—he's unreachable. True envy targets the ‘principal’ one chair ahead, close enough to grasp. This explains why sibling rivalry runs so deep: similar resources, closest distance. People envy friends, not celebrities. Envy only strikes in domains you genuinely care about—a cellist won't envy a tennis-champion friend. The pattern itself is information: what you envy, you can probably reach.

12:35 Jealousy is not a weakened version of envy; it's a different emotion
Kim clarifies an often-confused distinction. Jealousy (as a psychological term) requires three parties—the fear that someone important will transfer their attention, love, or admiration to a third party. Envy, by contrast, is wanting something someone else possesses that you lack. She illustrates with her own experience: in Korean culture, as an older sister to her younger brother who holds the status of 장손 (Jangson), the special position of the family's eldest male, she felt jealous of the extra attention he received. But she also envied his status—both emotions ran simultaneously.

14:44 SIREN: four questions about what jealousy really wants
Kim offers a tool called SIREN to disassemble jealousy: Similar goals, related domain, negative emotion, and most critically—‘the feeling behind the desire’. She illustrates with her daughter: the girl demands an iPhone, but deeper conversation reveals she doesn't actually want the device itself; she wants inclusion, the feeling of belonging with her peers. Another example: Kim envies a friend's renovated kitchen but can't renovate her own, so she buys an air fryer instead. Not recreating the whole kitchen, but finding an alternate path to that same feeling of ‘convenience’. The jealousy subsides when the underlying feeling is addressed, not when you acquire the exact object.

18:54 High achievement and competitive environments breed jealousy more easily
Kim references her conversations with researcher Robert Leahy: both observed in their clinical practices that jealousy surfaces more frequently among high-achievers and people in competitive environments—because they're constantly measuring themselves against others. Regarding whether women experience jealousy more than men, the research evidence is actually insufficient. The popular belief that ‘women are more envious’ persists more as conventional wisdom than fact; a more likely explanation is simply that women are more willing than men to admit feeling jealous.

22:04 Watch the desire itself, not the person
Kim identifies the boundary between malicious and benign jealousy: if your attention fixates on ‘that person’—wishing they'd lose what they have, or wanting to pull them down—the emotion trends malicious. But if attention centers on ‘the thing I want’ itself, jealousy becomes benign and mobilizing. For parents: guide children away from ‘who won the competition, who got the lead role’ and toward ‘what did they do to earn it?’ Treat the other person as a reference point toward your goal, not as an opponent to defeat.

25:11 When college admissions are rigged, look at who's beside you and behind you
Kim acknowledges that some contexts do contain structural unfairness—opaque admissions rules, people who leverage external advantages to sidestep the system. In those cases, simply ‘learning from the other person’ won't suffice. Her alternative: remember that on that upward ladder, people stand beside you and behind you, also reaching up. Humans habitually watch only one rung up, forgetting those below. ‘Linking arms’ with your neighbors—pulling each other up—may create limited change, but the act itself fills you with purpose rather than trapping you in ‘this is unfair.’

27:20 Used to envy the neighbor next door; now the phone compares 24/7
Social media has fundamentally altered the frequency of jealousy triggers: historically, people envied neighbors—those living in their world, nearby and visible. Now, unlocking your phone exposes you constantly to friends, acquaintances, even strangers' curated lives. The World Happiness Report shows Americans becoming less happy overall, with adolescent girls hit hardest. The issue isn't social comparison itself; it's the volume spinning out of control. The solution remains unchanged: learn to name ‘this is jealousy’, then ask what it's trying to tell you.

item.description: The PHP Foundation discovered this flaw two years ago but shelved the fix because nobody could prove it was exploitable. AI generated a complete remote-code-execution attack in a single day.
item.content:encoded:
The PHP Foundation discovered this flaw two years ago but shelved the fix because nobody could prove it was exploitable. AI generated a complete remote-code-execution attack in a single day.

A security CEO explains how AI has compressed vulnerability discovery and exploit generation from months to hours, using PHP and banking breaches as concrete examples of how defenders are now outpaced.

12:30 Superhuman Speed: Security Patches Scale from 20 to 1,400 Monthly
Microsoft once released roughly 20 security updates monthly; today that number has climbed to about 1,400 and keeps rising. Tasks that once required months and a full team to analyze can now be completed in days by one person with AI assistance. The guest argues this doesn't mean systems suddenly got weaker—it means AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation to near-superhuman speed, exposing years of accumulated technical debt all at once.

14:36 OpenAI Funds Vulnerability Discovery in Open-Source Projects
Calif joined OpenAI's Pass the Planet program—OpenAI funds and supplies compute credits to security firms to proactively discover and patch vulnerabilities in open-source software. Calif's team targeted PHP, pitched the idea to OpenAI and secured funding, then leveraged a former PHP security lead now at the firm to connect with the PHP Foundation and coordinate this joint vulnerability hunt.

18:42 The PHP Flaw Was Known Two Years Ago—Proof of Exploitation Was Missing
The PHP Foundation discovered the same vulnerability two years earlier but shelved the fix: remediation costs were prohibitive, the patch risked cascading breakage across dependent features, and without proof of exploitation nobody would justify the effort. After Calif's team rediscovered similar flaws, they used AI to generate working remote-code-execution payloads within days, then took this proof to the Foundation. Only then did the Foundation commit to the fix.

24:55 Well-Defended Systems Harbor Ten Times More Vulnerabilities Than Expected
PHP has never had a strong security reputation, so finding bugs there was unsurprising. What shocked the team was systems thought to have heavy security investment and proven trustworthiness: when tested with AI, they yielded roughly ten times more vulnerabilities than expected. The guest cites Chrome—defended intensively for years—which yielded hundreds of vulnerabilities to AI, surprising even Chrome's long-time security insiders.

33:10 Patches Turn Into Attack Windows Within Hours of Public Disclosure
Open-source fixes are committed publicly on GitHub; the moment a patch lands, attackers can diff the changes and reverse-engineer exploitable payloads within hours—what the guest calls a new breed of "minus-one-day" vulnerabilities. This attack window is narrowing across Windows, macOS, Python, Java, and nearly every critical software platform simultaneously, because threat actors are already watching patch drops and weaponizing them via AI in seconds.

37:13 Code-Generating AI Is Fundamentally Built to Be a Hacker
The guest dismisses the idea that AI can be trained not to attack: genuine code-generation skill requires understanding technical problems, debugging, and controlling machines—precisely what defines hacking. You cannot have one without the other. Moreover, AI companies' business model relies on selling tokens to programmers; short of exiting that market, they cannot train a coding-fluent model that won't eventually be weaponized.

42:19 What Took Months to Spread Now Spreads Across Networks in One Day
Calif describes a recent banking client hit by AI-driven attackers: where human operators once needed a month to propagate through a network, these actors penetrated Monday and compromised most of the enterprise by Tuesday—described as "cancer spreading at machine speed." OpenAI separately handled an incident with roughly 100 simultaneously-compromised nodes across one network, far above the typical one or two, rendering traditional single-node anomaly detection obsolete.

44:24 The Centaur-Hacker Era May Last Just Months Before Pure AI Takes Over
The guest draws a parallel to chess and Go: after Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997, human-AI "centaur" players dominated for roughly a decade before pure software took over; after AlphaGo, that transition compressed to three years. Calif believes hacking is now in its "centaur hacker" phase—AI plus human expertise is peak strength—but nobody knows how long it lasts: maybe three months, maybe three years.
